sections.title: What this site is
sections.html:
A static site refreshed every 15 minutes by GitHub Actions. It shows how the weather drives electricity demand and supply, and through them the prices, in France and Germany, using only free public data that can be fetched without a key. It observes, it does not model: every number is an observation, an official forecast, or a simple statistic on them (mean, median, straight-line fit, count). Where a series is missing the page says so.

Each chart has three blocks: What am I looking at?, Why does a trader care? and How is it computed?

sections.title: Weather indices
sections.html:
Temperature: 2 m temperature in 10 cities per country, weighted by rounded functional-urban-area population (Paris counts for about half of the French index). Wind: wind speed at 100 m on about 15 points per country placed on the main onshore and offshore wind areas, simple mean. Solar: global horizontal irradiance on about 10 sunny or well-equipped points per country, simple mean. No weights are learned from production data.

History comes from the Open-Meteo archive (ERA5 family reanalysis; the last few days from the ECMWF IFS analysis), forecasts from Open-Meteo's best-match model, the ensemble from ECMWF IFS ENS (51 members). Normals are the 2016–2025 mean for each day of the year, smoothed over ±15 days: a recent 10-year climate rather than the official 30-year normal, which suits a warming climate and keeps the data volume within the free quota.

sections.title: Power data
sections.html:
France: RTE éCO2mix via ODRÉ, definitive then consolidated then real-time data, joined without a gap (actuals every 30 minutes in definitive data, 15 minutes in real time). Germany: load and load forecast from SMARD (Bundesnetzagentur), generation by fuel from Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE). Day-ahead prices for all zones from Energy-Charts. Installed capacities from Energy-Charts (monthly for Germany, yearly for France, last value carried forward).

Residual load = consumption − wind − solar. Capacity factor = output ÷ installed capacity.

sections.title: Rules of thumb shown
sections.html: The demand effect of a temperature anomaly uses RTE's published order of magnitude for France (about 2.4 GW per °C in winter) and, for Germany, the heating slope measured on the Weather → Demand page. They are shown as orders of magnitude, never as a forecast.

sections.title: Flexibility: bots and battery (from v1)
sections.html:
Each bot holds p ∈ {−1, 0, +1} MW on Belgian quarter-hour Q, bought or sold at the day-ahead price and settled at the Elia imbalance price:

pnl = p × (imbalance_price − DA_BE) × 0.25 h − 0.5 €/MWh × |p| × 0.25 h

Decisions are taken 20 minutes before Q with real-time data up to Q−3 only, and Elia SI-forecast vintages published before the decision. The rule bot goes long when Elia's next-quarter-hour SI forecast says the system is short (SI < 0), short when it is long. The ML bot is a LightGBM classifier of the sign of (imbalance − DA), retrained every Monday on data published before the cut-off. A unit test scrambles everything outside the information set and checks the decisions do not change. Live decisions are appended to a CSV journal that is never rewritten.

Most of the backtest edge comes from the persistence of the Belgian imbalance spread; it is not capturable at scale (a BRP must stay balanced, large deviations move the price). The live record is the measure that matters.

Battery League: 1 MW / 2 MWh, 88% round-trip efficiency, at most 2 cycles a day, solved per zone and day as a linear programme on day-ahead prices with perfect foresight. A theoretical maximum.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.html:
• No continuous intraday prices, TTF or EUA prices: they are not free (see Data Hub → Data gaps).
  • Grid-mean wind and radiation are crude: one number cannot describe a country, so power curves are wide.
  • French installed capacity is yearly: capacity factors in the current year are slightly overstated as new solar is connected.
  • Paper trading only for the bots; the battery is a perfect-foresight maximum.
  • Freshness depends on GitHub's cron punctuality and on each source's publication delay.
